summary:
Every lunar mission carries a quiet fear: that the crew may not come home. Landings still fail, as Apollo 11’s descent alarms, Luna-25, and IM-2 showed, and the usual answer is to abort, which wastes years of work. Our website helps teams choose safer landings at the Moon’s south pole and respond when something goes wrong.
The planning side offers a 3D Moon, Earth, and Sun view, landmark sites with their characteristics, sunset and Earthset countdowns, and a lunar-day timeline with terrain-based horizons. It also ranks compared sites and lists backup sites within 1.5 km. The emergency simulator shows which surface points a spacecraft can still reach with its remaining fuel, drawing a footprint over real terrain.

details:
For an astronaut, being chosen for a lunar mission is a moment of pure excitement. But that joy always carries a quieter thought, the possibility of never coming home, and every astronaut’s family lives with it too. Our project exists for that thought.

The danger is not abstract. In 1969, Apollo 11’s landing computer raised alarms during descent, and the crew had to fly past their planned site to find safer ground. In 2023, Russia’s Luna-25 crashed during its descent, and in 2025 Intuitive Machines’ IM-2 tipped over near the Moon’s south pole. Landings still go wrong, and when they do, crews and controllers have seconds to decide where to go. Historically the answer to a failure was to abort the mission. That protects the crew, but it throws away years of work and the scientific goals behind it. Our solution is a website that helps teams choose landing sites well before launch and gives them a way to evaluate alternatives if something goes wrong. It focuses on the Moon’s south pole, where lighting and communication conditions are extreme and where future crewed missions are headed.

The first half of the website is built for planning. Its interface centers on a zoomable 3D model of the Moon, Earth, and Sun with their orbits. A “show landmarks” button displays Apollo sites, CLPS targets, commercial missions, and sites from other countries’ programs, and users can click any landmark, or any point on the Moon, to see its slope, terrain smoothness, luminosity, mineral content, and optimal Earth transmission period. They can also enter the characteristics they want and let the program find the best match. A calendar and time bar at the bottom lets the user choose a mission date and time, and the program then shows the time remaining before sunset and Earthset, along with a timeline of how conditions change across the lunar day. These calculations use terrain-based horizons, so hills and crater walls that block the Sun or Earth are accounted for. Color-coded overlays show patterns such as mineral or water abundance at a glance, and users can compare two or more points and receive a ranking with explanations. Finally, a “vicinity” button lists backup sites within 1.5 km that resemble the chosen site, ranked from best to worst, so a mission can be prepared for a deviation.

The second half answers the question that matters most when something fails in the air: with the fuel that is left, where can we still go? Our landing simulator shows which surface points a spacecraft can still reach if it must change course. The user enters the craft’s position, height above the terrain, horizontal speed, wet mass, fuel as a percentage of mass, maximum thrust, propellant energy, engine efficiency, and maximum flight time, and can import a topographic map. The simulator builds a landing footprint over the real terrain, marking which points are within the fuel budget and which are not, and leaving gray any area where no valid path exists. Clicking a target draws its flight path in 3D, and the path can be exported.

Together, these two halves solve the problem from both ends. The planning tools remove the need to juggle several specialist programs, so planners can compare sites and dates quickly, even after a launch delay. The simulator gives teams a way to think through a failure before it happens. The result is a shift from “abort or hope” toward informed alternatives that keep both the crew and the mission goals in view.

The tool is built on real data. Sun and Earth positions come from Stellarium, and terrain comes from NASA’s Lunar Orbiter Laser Altimeter (LOLA) topographic maps. The reach calculation is a simplified general model of how far the available fuel can carry a lander, and we state that limit openly. It does not yet cover the return trip to Earth, which is the next development step for real missions.

Today the tool serves mission planners and engineering teams, who can import their own topographic maps for professional use. Educators and space enthusiasts can use it too, because the data is already interpreted and no one has to read raw ephemeris tables. In the future, the tool could become onboard software that calculates reachable sites in real time from a specific spacecraft’s fuel, mission, and design, and could join the two halves into one ranking of sites that are both safe and scientifically valuable.

Public interest matters here too. Apollo 11 drew enormous attention, but audiences drifted away until Apollo 13’s oxygen tank explosion put three lives at risk. Missions depend on funding, and funding depends on people caring. A tool that puts crew safety at the center keeps the human story at the center of lunar exploration.
